description_full: Tokio Marine Holdings, Inc. engages in the non-life and life insurance, and financial and general businesses in Japan, the United States, and internationally. The company provides personal lines, accident and health, absence management, workers' compensation, retirement services, energy, renewables, property, natural catastrophes, aviation and space, commercial auto/motor, fine arts and specie, agriculture TNC, equestrian and blood stock, life sciences, financial lines, professional indemnity, surety, liability, professional liability, IP, political risk/violence and terrorism, trade/business interruption, product recall, cyber, crisis management insurance, contingency and events, stop loss, treaty reinsurance, business package, contractors all risks, trade credit, Japanese business, high net worth, urban and spatial development, and consulting solutions; marine, cargo, and hull; nonprofit, education, and human services; and sports entertainment, and leisure solutions. It also operates in various business areas comprising non-life insurance/PC, life insurance, reinsurance, asset management, risk management services, professional service, health and wellness, financial services, insurance related services, solution business for social issues. The company was formerly known as Millea Holdings, Inc. and changed its name to Tokio Marine Holdings, Inc. in 2008. Tokio Marine Holdings, Inc. was founded in 1879 and is headquartered in Chiyoda, Japan.

financial_summary: Tokio Marine Holdings, Inc. is a large-cap financial services business with a $102.4B market cap on $50.1B of annual revenue.

The business throws off $7.8B in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.62× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
